questions.text:
Choose ONE context from the Resource Booklet:
• Context One: Sleep quality and screen time (Resource A: a university health research centre report; Resource B: a technology company's wellness blog)
• Context Two: Native tree planting and carbon capture (Resource A: a Department of Conservation factsheet; Resource B: a commercial carbon-offset company's website)

Use Resource A from your chosen context to respond to the following:

(a) Who published this information?

(b) Why was this information published?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify who published the information and why
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describe the source and its intended purpose. Context One: (a) Researchers at a university health research centre published this report. (b) They published it to inform the public about research findings linking screen time before bed to reduced sleep quality. Context Two: (a) The Department of Conservation (DOC) published this factsheet. (b) They published it to educate the public about the role of native trees in capturing and storing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

questions.text: (c) What is a science-related claim in this resource?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify a science-related claim from the resource
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describe a science-related claim in the information. Context One examples: Exposure to blue light from screens before bedtime suppresses melatonin production. People who use devices within one hour of bedtime take longer to reach deep sleep. Context Two examples: Established native forest can absorb up to 3.6 tonnes of CO₂ per hectare per year. Planting native species such as tōtara and kahikatea creates long-term carbon sinks that persist for centuries.

questions.text: (d) What are the science language or conventions used in support of this claim?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify and explain how science language and conventions are used to support the claim
questions.markingGuide: Merit: Show understanding and describe the science-related claims, explaining how science language or conventions support them. Context One: Science language — melatonin, circadian rhythm, blue-light wavelength (450–490 nm), REM sleep. Science conventions — sample size of 412 participants; controlled sleep study; data presented as mean hours of sleep with standard deviation; peer-reviewed journal article from 2023. Using specific wavelengths and a large sample makes the findings more credible. The researchers' university affiliation adds authority. Context Two: Science language — carbon sequestration, photosynthesis, biomass, carbon sink, CO₂ per hectare. Science conventions — data measured in tonnes of CO₂ per hectare per year; data gathered over a 20-year monitoring period; DOC is a government-funded organisation with expertise in ecology. Long-term measurements and standardised units strengthen the claim.

questions.text: (e) How well do the science language or conventions used in the information support the claim that you identified in part (c)? Use evidence to support your response.
questions.expectedAnswer: Evaluate how well the science language/conventions support the claim, discussing strengths and weaknesses
questions.markingGuide: Excellence: Evaluate the use of science language or conventions used to support the science-related claims. Context One: The study uses a reasonably large sample size (412), which makes the results more generalisable. The research was published in a peer-reviewed journal, meaning other experts have checked the methodology and conclusions. However, the study only measured short-term effects (two weeks), so we cannot be certain whether these effects persist long-term. The participants were all university students aged 18–24, which limits how well the findings apply to other age groups. Despite this, the use of precise scientific measurements (melatonin levels in saliva, sleep onset latency in minutes) makes the data reliable and the claim well-supported. Context Two: DOC is a government department with no financial interest in selling carbon offsets, so their motivation is likely to inform rather than persuade. The 20-year monitoring period provides strong longitudinal evidence. However, the factsheet does not explain the methodology used to measure carbon absorption, and the figure of 3.6 tonnes per hectare is an average that may vary significantly depending on soil type, rainfall, and species mix. There is also no mention of peer review for the specific data cited. Overall, the claim is reasonably well supported by the science language and conventions, but more detail about the measurement methods would strengthen it.

questions.text:
Use Resource B from your chosen context to respond to the following:

(a) Who published this information?

(b) Why was this information published?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify who published the information and why
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describe the source and intended purpose. Context One: (a) A technology company published this on their wellness blog. (b) They published this to promote their device's built-in 'night mode' feature and to appear health-conscious. Context Two: (a) A commercial carbon-offset company published this on their website. (b) The purpose was to convince people to purchase carbon credits by planting native trees.

questions.text: (c) What is a science-related claim in this resource?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify a science-related claim from the resource
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Describe a science-related claim. Context One examples: Their night-mode feature reduces blue-light emission by 70%, which the company claims significantly improves sleep quality. Context Two examples: Planting one native tree offsets 50 kg of CO₂ emissions per year, and their planting programme is the most effective way to reduce your personal carbon footprint.

questions.text: (d) What are the science language or conventions used in support of this claim?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify and explain how science language and conventions support the claim
questions.markingGuide: Merit: Show understanding and describe the science-related claims, explaining how science language or conventions support them. Context One: Science language — blue-light spectrum, circadian rhythm, melatonin. Science conventions — the blog cites a percentage (70% reduction) but does not reference the study it came from; no author name or qualifications listed; the company also sells the product being promoted, creating a potential conflict of interest. The use of percentages makes the claim sound precise, but without a source, the reader cannot verify it. Context Two: Science language — carbon offset, CO₂ emissions, carbon footprint, native biodiversity. Science conventions — the figure of 50 kg per tree per year is presented without a source; the company profits from selling carbon credits, creating a conflict of interest; no date given for when the data was collected; no mention of independent verification or peer review. The science-sounding language may give readers false confidence in the accuracy of the claims.

questions.text: (e) How well do the science language or conventions used in the information support the claim that you identified in part (c)? Use evidence to support your response.
questions.expectedAnswer: Evaluate how well the science language/conventions support the claim, discussing strengths and weaknesses
questions.markingGuide: Excellence: Evaluate the use of science language or conventions used to support science-related claims. Context One: The company has a clear commercial motivation — they are selling the very product they claim improves sleep. This conflict of interest means they are unlikely to report any negative findings about their product. The 70% reduction figure sounds impressive but is not linked to any published study. Without knowing the experimental conditions, we cannot assess whether this reduction is meaningful for real-world sleep improvement. However, the use of scientifically accurate terms like 'melatonin' and 'circadian rhythm' shows some familiarity with the science, which could make the claim seem more trustworthy to a reader. Overall, the claim lacks the supporting evidence needed to be considered scientifically robust. Context Two: The company is selling carbon credits, so they have a financial incentive to overstate the benefits of tree planting. The claim that one tree offsets 50 kg of CO₂ per year is a very specific figure that sounds credible, but without knowing the tree species, age, growing conditions, or measurement method, it is impossible to verify. The language used (carbon footprint, native biodiversity, carbon offset) is accurate but may be used strategically to make the product seem environmentally responsible. An independent audit or peer-reviewed research supporting their figures would significantly strengthen the claim. Without this, the claim remains commercially motivated and only partially supported by the science language used.
